design: Instrument development informed by a systematic scoping review, expert proposals and empirical observations
prior_exposure: The investigator and coding assistant have seen existing instruments, prior Gen-2 drafts and a colleague's QA suggestion. This is not a claim of hypothesis-free discovery or blinded authorship.
conduct_framework: JBI scoping review guidance, full-text verification pending
appraisal: Item-level evidence mapping informed by COSMIN principles; adaptations to documentation checklists explicitly recorded. No automatic alpha, CVR, factor-analysis or agreement threshold determines content validity.
questions: Which properties of useful and accurate psychotherapy documentation are defined in the literature and professional guidance?
For which recipients, purposes and clinical circumstances do those properties matter?
How are they operationalized and what evidence supports their measurement?
What transfers to automated English and Czech evaluation and what remains unvalidated?

pcc.population: Human-written and model-generated psychotherapy session documentation; adjacent clinical documentation and summarization methods identified as transfer evidence
pcc.concept: Documentation quality constructs, operational criteria and measurement properties
pcc.context: Continuity of care and documentation. The search of 2026-09-13 covered supervision and client communication as well, and their findings are retained; from 2026-09-16 the instrument is built for the two purposes above only (decision D8).

date_limits.upper: actual search date recorded for each execution

include: Psychotherapy progress notes or session summaries with explicit quality properties, user needs or evaluation methods
Clinical documentation or general summarization methods with an explicit documentation measurement application, labelled as transfer evidence
Professional or recipient requirements with attributable authorship, jurisdiction and document version
Full text in English or Czech, including preprints and software artifacts with publication type explicitly distinguished
exclude: Therapeutic chatbot or treatment effectiveness evaluation without a documentation-relevant requirement or method
No identifiable quality construct, operational criterion or measurement method
Duplicate report with no additional evidence, linked to its study family rather than counted independently
Full text outside English/Czech scope, with the language restriction disclosed

judge_question_granularity.what_varies: how many operational items one judge call decides: batched, every item of a reference mode in one call, as pipeline.score asks today; or split, one item per call, as generation 1's judge asks

guards_before_measurement.what_this_is: Checks run on a note before any measure is computed over it, and on a ratio before it is published. They exist because a benchmark creates the incentive it measures: whatever is scored is what a system will be built to maximise, and some measures can be maximised without the note getting better.
guards_before_measurement.already_in_the_code: fraction() returns no number when the denominator is zero, so nothing is reported rather than 1.00 or 0.00, and an empty note has its own branch in pipeline.score: its answers are recorded as not_in_note and its QA verdicts as omitted, not as correct. Both come from the rule that an absence is never a measurement.
guards_before_measurement.missing_and_declared_here: There is no floor above zero. A one-sentence note has a denominator of one, so its economy is 1.00 -- the best possible score for the emptiest possible note, which is the trap the sheet uses as its worked example.
guards_before_measurement.the_rule: Every ratio is published with the denominator it was computed over. A ratio whose denominator is below the floor is reported as not computed, with the denominator beside it, and never as a value. This is the rule that an absence is never a measurement, extended: a ratio over almost nothing is not a measurement either.
guards_before_measurement.the_floor_comes_from_the_pilot: Not guessed. The pilot's notes give the distribution of denominators and the floor is set from it, in the same amendment that fixes the confirmatory sample size. Until it exists no ratio from this instrument is published.
guards_before_measurement.where_more_guards_come_from: The panel's second question. A gaming shape a rater names becomes a candidate guard, and the paper reports which ones were named, which were built and which were left.

decision_ledger.decision: An information unit is graded on the five levels of TN-Eval's Appendix C (mandatory, mandatory in certain circumstances, highly recommended, good to have, optional), taken verbatim. Coverage is reported per grade, one measure each. The core carried three grades of its own (essential, supplementary, not_required) and they are gone.
decision_ledger.replaces: the three grades the core package was written with, which predate the review that found the five
affects: the bank sheet: the therapist assigns one of five grades per purpose, not one of three
coverage: five recall measures where there were two, each with its own denominator
the judge prompt, which is told the grades it may use
aggregation-v5: the shape of what measure() returns changed, so an older manifest is archived rather than recalculated
decision_ledger.why: The three grades could not carry out the severity rule the pilot runs on. That rule separates the omission of an optional unit (no error) from a good-to-have one (minor) from a highly recommended or mandatory one (major), and three grades cannot tell those apart. The five also have the only reliability figure in the grading: five therapists agreed on them at Fleiss' kappa 0.68 and Krippendorff's alpha 0.73. The three had none, and were not a simplification anyone had tested. Coverage had also been reporting two of the three, so units at the third grade were neither counted nor declared missing, which is the shape this project treats as a defect wherever it appears.
decision_ledger.costs_nothing_published: No published number used this grading: of the 2357 result rows, none carries QA coverage. Generation 2 is a separate instrument from the leaderboard, so no comparability group is split by the change.
decision_ledger.not_decided_here: Whether the other three branches of the severity rule are enforced in code. They stay prose the rater reads, because a severity derived from the grade would record agreement with the rule rather than the rater's reading of the note.

decision_ledger.decision: How many items one judge call decides is a condition of the pilot, measured, not chosen in advance. On the eight notes of the human sample every operational item is asked twice: once batched, as the pipeline asks today, with every item of a reference mode in one call, and once split, one item per call, as generation 1's judge asks. The confirmatory round uses whichever the pilot supports, and the comparison is reported either way.
decision_ledger.replaces: the batched call as an unexamined property of the code; it was never decided, it was written
affects: the pilot: a second pass over the human-sample notes for every judge family, which is judge calls and no generation calls
the confirmatory round's judge-call budget, which the two styles differ on by about a factor of five
the pipeline's assess step, which takes a tuple of items and has no way to be asked one at a time
decision_ledger.why: Generation 1 asks one question per call and says so in the first line of its judge module: roughly 60 calls per note, 23 rubric criteria, one per sentence for conciseness, twelve Likert ratings. Generation 2's pipeline asks every item of a reference mode at once, roughly 6 calls per note. The two generations therefore disagree about the one thing that decides whether a verdict is any good, and neither choice was ever measured against the other here. Asking it of the pilot costs a few hundred judge calls and nothing on e-INFRA, and the pilot already holds the two things the comparison needs: a human anchor on eight notes and blind repeats that measure the judge's own noise.
decision_ledger.rule_declared_in_advance: The split asking is adopted for the confirmatory round if its agreement with the human anchor exceeds the batched asking's by more than the judge's own blind-repeat disagreement on the same items. Below that margin the batched asking is kept, because a difference smaller than the instrument's own noise is not a finding. Either way both figures are published, and a pilot too small to separate them is reported as that and not as agreement.
decision_ledger.not_decided_here: Whether the split asking is better. That is what the condition measures. Nor is the number of items: the pool may still grow before the panel answers, and the style question is about how many items share a call rather than how many exist.

decision_ledger.decision: A criterion enters the measured set only where all three raters answer quite or highly relevant. Two of three no longer retains it: the item is published as contested, with both the agreeing and the dissenting reasons, and is not measured in this round. The sheet names the cut, says that a blank is not a vote, and shows what each property is judged over. Agreement is reported as Krippendorff's alpha over the three raters' ordinal answers with the three pairwise Cohen's kappas beside it.
decision_ledger.replaces: the rule recorded on 2026-10-07, under which two of three retained the item and marked it contested, and which named Cohen's kappa for a panel of three
affects: the measured set: an item two raters call relevant and one does not is reported and not measured, where it would have been measured and marked
the sheet the three raters receive: the cut, the blank rule, the renamed third step and a column saying what the property is judged over
the agreement figure in the paper, which is now alpha with the pairwise kappas beside it rather than a kappa that was not defined for three raters
decision_ledger.why: Four points with the cut above the midpoint means a rater choosing uniformly calls an item relevant half the time. Under that null two of three agreeing has probability 0.50, so the old rule retained an item as often as a coin would; unanimity among three has probability 0.125. Three of five would be 0.50 again, so the problem was the cut and not the number of raters. The investigator asked for three raters and an unambiguous verdict, and unanimity is the only cut among three that gives one.
decision_ledger.the_null_these_figures_assume: a rater choosing uniformly among the four points, which describes nobody. The figures are a floor for reading the index, not an estimate of how this panel behaves, and the paper states the null wherever it quotes them. A real rater's answers are not independent of the item, which is the whole reason to ask them.
decision_ledger.what_this_costs: Items that two of three call relevant. Under the old rule they were measured and flagged; now they are reported and not measured, so the measured set can only be smaller. That is the intended direction: the round claims a screening of the pool, and an item that one in three experts does not consider relevant to note quality is not something to publish a number about.
decision_ledger.not_decided_here: Whether a contested item returns in a second round. The pool may not grow once an answer exists, so a contested item waits for a panel that is asked again, and no such panel is planned.

decision_ledger.decision: Lynn (1986) and Davis (1992) are read and quoted where the panel rests on them. The retention rule stays exactly as D19 set it, and is now reported with Lynn's Table 2 beside it rather than as this project's own convention alone; the panel of three is reported with Lynn's floor of three and its condition; and the scale's labels are reported as not Lynn's, with the question of whether they are Davis's left open and named.

Three of this project's own decisions are in them and one of its claims is contradicted, and a protocol that had said the sources were unread could not say either.
decision_ledger.the_order_of_events_is_part_of_the_recor: The unanimity rule was decided on 2026-10-21 from the chance levels of a four-point scale, and Lynn was read on 2026-10-22. A reader who wants to discount the agreement can.

decision_ledger.replaces: a single contested tier, four scale steps with no anchors, a sheet with no examples, and a column header that asked whether the property could do harm
affects: what is reported about an item two raters accept: two outcomes where there was one
the sheet: an example column, four anchor lines, a repaired harm header and the answer columns moved from E, F, G to F, G, H
the time the sheet asks of a rater, which rises from an estimated 30 minutes to 45
decision_ledger.why: The investigator asked why the scale is not simply yes or no, and answered it: with a binary you cannot tell agreement from indecision. That is only true if the four points are used for something, and they were not -- the rule collapsed them to the cut and nothing else read them. Now the tier an item lands in depends on the third rater's step, so the resolution is paid for. The anchors and the examples are the same argument at the other end: a rater asked to judge 'non-stigmatising language' from one sentence, on a scale of four undefined adjectives, is not being asked a question that has an answer.
decision_ledger.the_precedent: MentalHealthBench (OpenAI, 2026) built its rubrics with more than 80 licensed clinicians and keeps a criterion where at least two of three experts agree and the third does not contradict it. That is the middle tier here. It is not adopted as the retention rule, because their third expert adjudicates and ours does not, and because three raters rating a fixed pool is a weaker design than eighty authoring criteria.
decision_ledger.not_decided_here: Whether a contested item of either tier returns in a second round. No second panel is planned.

decision_ledger.decision: The panel is four raters. An item enters the measured set only where all four answer quite or highly relevant; three of four is published as contested in two tiers by what the fourth said, and two or fewer removes it. Each rater rates every criterion twice, once for a progress note and once for a therapeutic note, on separate tabs whose order alternates between raters. The sheet states what the instrument is for and which note type each tab asks about.
decision_ledger.replaces: a panel of three rating one undifferentiated session note, and the served purposes continuity and audit
affects: the retention rule, whose chance level falls from 0.125 to 0.0625
what each rater is asked: 78 judgements instead of 39, an estimated 45 minutes a tab
the served purposes: audit leaves the round and a therapeutic note enters it
every relevance value in the catalog, which is the assistant's and which the panel's answers replace for these two note types
decision_ledger.why: The investigator named four raters and asked for the two note types to be rated apart. Both improve the instrument: four raters halve the chance level of the retention rule, and two tabs measure the thing the round is actually about, which is that a property essential to a note the care team reads may be pointless in a note the clinician keeps for themselves. Rating them in two columns of one tab would have produced a second answer anchored on the first.
decision_ledger.the_purposes_are_not_the_code_s_purposes: What the code calls `continuity` -- 'enable a therapist to resume care safely at the next session' -- is the progress note under another name, and the sheet records that mapping. The therapeutic note has no profile in the code. `audit` leaves the served set: it is a payer's view of a progress note, not a second genre of note. The identifiers appear in 264 places and are not renamed here; the rename is due before the pilot runs, and the pilot has not run.
decision_ledger.not_decided_here: How a contested item is treated if the two tabs disagree about it -- essential as a progress note and not as a therapeutic note is not a contested item, it is the finding. The reporting of that case is written when the answers exist.

decision_ledger.decision: The rating tab carries the table and nothing above it. Each criterion shows one example, the failing case. A legend tab holds what a rater needs and cannot get elsewhere: one sentence for each of the two note types, what they are looking at, and what the four steps of the scale mean. Everything else -- how long it takes, what happens to the answers, that each copy is private -- goes in the message that carries the link, in the sender's own words.
decision_ledger.replaces: twenty-nine rows of preamble above the first criterion, a heading repeating the tab's own name, and a pair of examples in every row
affects: what a rater reads before answering, which falls from twenty-nine rows to none
the example column, which holds the failing case alone and is named for it
the relevance answers, in a direction named below
decision_ledger.why: The investigator read the built sheet and refused it. Most of the preamble was written for a reviewer of this paper and the protocol already holds every line of it: the chance levels, the amendment dates, the reason the order is shuffled. On a participant's sheet those say that we are guarding against them answering at random. The note type was stated twice on one screen, in the tab's name and in a heading under it. And two examples a row, over thirty-nine rows and two tabs, is reading that buys nothing the one failing example does not.
decision_ledger.what_the_single_example_costs: A column of nothing but failures makes every property look like a live problem, which can only push a relevance answer upward. The pair was neutral in that respect and unreadable in every other. There is no unbiased single example: the positive one alone would push the other way and says nothing at all for a criterion written as the absence of a fault. The direction is named here, in the paper, and beside any count of retained items.
decision_ledger.not_decided_here: Whether the bias is large enough to matter. Nothing measures it, and with one panel nothing can; a second round shown positive examples would, and none is planned.

decision_ledger.decision: The harm question leaves the table and is asked once under it, beside the question about what the list is missing, with a worked example: a one-sentence note scores 1.00 on economy, so grading economy by itself rewards writing almost nothing. A rater who sees such a trap names the criterion and says how; there is no per-item answer.
decision_ledger.replaces: a column of thirty-nine cells on each tab, and a legend entry whose example was invented
affects: what a rater fills in: two cells a row instead of three, and one box at the end
the retention rule's harm flag, which now reads a criterion the rater names
the sheet, which has seven columns
decision_ledger.why: Thirty-eight of thirty-nine cells would have stayed empty on each of two tabs, and a rater had to carry a second question through every row to produce them. The investigator also refused the explanation that went with it, correctly: it claimed a model graded on non-stigmatising language would stop recording that a client is at risk, and that does not follow, because recording risk is a clinical description and not a label on a person. The example had been invented to sound convincing.
decision_ledger.what_is_lost: A rater is no longer prompted at the moment they read each criterion, so a trap that would have occurred to them in passing may not occur to them at the end. Nothing measures how much that costs. What is kept is the question, its rule and a case that shows what is being asked, which the column did not have.
decision_ledger.and_the_scale_gains_an_answer_that_is_no: The rater may answer 'nevim', I cannot judge this. It is coded as missing and not as a fifth point on the ordinal axis: Krippendorff's alpha is defined for incomplete data and drops a unit with fewer than two answers, which costs nothing, while a fifth step would make the distance between the four mean nothing. The outcome for the item is what a blank already gave -- not rated by all four, so not measured -- and what is gained is knowing the criterion was read and found unjudgeable rather than skipped.
decision_ledger.not_decided_here: Whether a criterion many raters cannot judge should be rewritten or dropped. With one panel there is no second reading to compare it with.

decision_ledger.decision: The panel's second question asks how a model could win on a criterion without the note being better, and keeps the broader harm as its second clause. Separately, a ratio is not a measurement when its denominator is too small: every published ratio carries the denominator it was computed over, and one below the floor is reported as not computed rather than as 1.00 or 0.00. The floor is set from the pilot and is not guessed here.
decision_ledger.replaces: a question asking whether measuring a property could mislead or harm, which the investigator could not parse, and a ratio that reports 1.00 over a denominator of one
affects: the sheet's second open question, which now leads with gaming
every ratio the instrument publishes, which gains its denominator
the pilot, which has to produce the floor before any ratio is published
decision_ledger.why: A rater can answer how a model would win on something; whether measuring it could mislead is a question about our instrument asked in our words. And the example that makes it concrete is a gaming shape, not a harm in general: a one-sentence note scores 1.00 on economy because the sentence it has does carry content. The guard belongs in the measurement because that shape is known in advance; the question is for the shapes that are not.
decision_ledger.the_two_are_not_the_same: Gaming is the part of harm that has a shape, and not all of it. Coverage cannot be gamed by including more, it is satisfied by it, and what pays is privacy, through K15. A guard cannot catch that: nothing in a note that honestly covers more looks wrong. Which is why the question keeps its second clause and the two run together.
decision_ledger.what_the_guard_does_not_do: It catches a shape somebody thought of. The panel's answers are where the shapes nobody thought of are supposed to come from, and each one named there becomes a candidate guard rather than a finding on its own.
decision_ledger.not_decided_here: The floor itself. A ratio over one sentence means nothing and a ratio over fifty means something; where it turns is an empirical question the pilot answers, and writing a number here would be the guess this project keeps removing from other people's work.

content_validity.status: registered before any rating exists; no answer has been collected and no sheet has been sent. The pool was 34 items when the rule was registered and is larger now; catalog/catalog.json holds the list the sheet is built from, and the sheet takes its count from that list rather than stating one.

procedure.named: expert rating of the item pool for relevance, with a retention threshold declared in advance; a screening round of a modified Delphi
source_quotes: Multiple judges have been used (typically ranging from 5 to 7)
an increase in the number of experts has been found to increase the robustness of the ratings
procedure.what_the_source_recommends: S12 names three ways to quantify the judges' assessments, the content validity ratio, the content validity index and Cohen's kappa, and recommends kappa as the most efficient. The numeric thresholds conventionally used with the first two come from Lawshe (1975), which this project has not retrieved and takes nothing from, and Lynn (1986), which it read on 2026-10-22 through the university's proxy. What Lynn's Table 2 requires of three experts is the rule this project had already adopted a day earlier on its own argument: all three. The quotes are in research/gen2/panel-scale-sources.json, with what each one settles and what was not read beside it.

panel.profile: psychotherapy researchers or practising therapists, none of them the instrument's author and none the assistant
panel.identities: held locally; a rater is named in the paper only with their consent
panel.independence_to_record_per_rater: whether the rater will be an author of the paper, because a rater who will be an author is not an independent judge and must be reported as a co-author's rating
panel.below_the_typical_range: S12 calls five to seven typical and this panel is three. Lynn (1986), the source S12 cites for the content validity index, names three as the floor: 'in content/domain areas of sufficient restriction to preclude large numbers of experts, a minimum of three experts should be used', and calls two 'not only statistically unjustifiable' but a risk of concluding that content validity is absent when it is not. Three is therefore a floor this project meets rather than simply fewer than typical -- on a condition it has to argue rather than assume, that the domain precludes more. The arithmetic is coarse at three either way, and the round is still reported as a screening of the pool and not as established content validity.
panel.independence_of_the_ratings: each rater answers on their own copy and sees no other rater's answers; a shared sheet would make the second and third answer a reaction to the first
panel.design: Four raters, each rating every criterion twice: once for a progress note and once for a therapeutic note, on separate tabs rather than in two columns, because an answer made beside the previous one is an answer about it. Which tab comes first alternates between raters, two and two, so that fatigue does not accumulate on the same note type and read as a difference between them. Lynn (1986) requires all four of four in the same table that requires all three of three, so the rule is unchanged in kind by the extra rater and stricter in effect.

what_is_rated.items: every candidate of the catalog, including those the round does not measure, the one the investigator dropped on 2026-10-05, and K35 and K36, which arrived on 2026-10-07 from a source read in full
what_is_rated.shown_per_item: the code, the Czech name, one sentence of definition, one example -- the failing case, from the catalog -- and what the property is judged over, which is one note for thirty-six of them, several sessions with one client for one and a model across clients for two; no state, no origin, no citation, no measurement rule and no indication of what the assistant or the investigator thinks. The table is the first row of the tab: what stood above it until 2026-10-22 is under framing below.
what_is_rated.why_blind_to_state: The sheet carries the code, the Czech name, one sentence, the catalog's positive and negative example, and what the property is judged over. It carries no state, no origin, no citation, no measurement rule and none of this project's own relevance ratings. That is the sheet; it is not a controlled condition. The whole catalog, including those ratings, is on a published page, and nothing prevents a rater from finding it. The investigator states that none of the three has seen that page, and the sheet asks them not to look the criteria up before answering. Both of those are reported as what they are -- his statement and a request -- and not as blinding that anyone enforced.
what_is_rated.pool_changes_before_the_panel: A pool may grow until the first sheet is sent, and two items were added on 2026-10-07. After an answer exists it may not: adding an item then would mean some raters rated it and others did not, and the threshold is a proportion of three. If a property is found after the panel has answered, it waits for a second round and is reported as a later addition.

purposes_rated.progress_note: Part of the record. The care team that takes over and the payer read it, and the client has a right of access to it. This is the purpose the code calls `continuity`, under a name that says what the note is rather than what it is for.
purposes_rated.therapeutic_note: The clinician's own analysis of the session, kept apart from the record, not written to be handed over or billed. Under 45 CFR 164.501 a psychotherapy note is excluded from the client's right of access and excludes by name diagnosis, functional status, treatment plan, symptoms, prognosis and progress, which belong in the record. The code has no profile for it.
purposes_rated.audit_leaves_the_round: A documentation audit is a payer's or an auditor's view of a progress note, not a second genre of note, so it is not one of the two the panel is asked about. The investigator's objection recorded against K07 proposed exactly this pair.
purposes_rated.what_this_does_to_the_catalog: Every candidate carries a relevance value per purpose and every one of them is the assistant's. For these two note types the panel's answers replace them, which is the first time any of those values will have come from somebody qualified to make it. Until the answers exist the catalog's values stand and are labelled as the assistant's wherever they are published.

what_is_rated.framing: Not on the sheet. Until 2026-10-22 the sheet opened with twenty-nine rows that said what the instrument is for and a good deal besides -- the chance levels of the retention rule, the dates of this protocol's amendments, why the criteria are shuffled -- and the investigator refused all of it: a participant's sheet that explains the guard against random answering is telling four experienced therapists what we suspect them of. The orientation Davis (1992) asks for is in the message that carries the link, in the sender's own words, and the legend tab holds the two things a rater cannot get elsewhere: what they are looking at, and what the four steps mean. The sentences are in research/gen2/catalog/czech.json and the ones that left are kept there with their dates.

questions.text: Is this relevant to the quality of a psychotherapy session note?
questions.scale_source: Four points with the cut above the midpoint is Lynn's (1986), read on 2026-10-22: 'the 4-point scale is preferable because it does not include the ambivalent middle rating common in odd number rating scales', and Davis (1992) computes the index from 'the total number of items ranked 3 or 4 by both reviewers'. The labels are not Lynn's, whose third and fourth options are 'relevant but needs minor alteration' and 'very relevant and succinct' -- about what to do with the item, not only about how relevant it is. Whether this project's wording is Davis's is unsettled: the figure that would settle it was not read, which research/gen2/panel-scale-sources.json records as unread. Lawshe (1975) remains unretrieved and nothing is taken from it.
questions.anchors: Each step carries a sentence saying what it means, in research/gen2/catalog/czech.json under vocabulary.relevance_scale, and the sheet builds those lines from there. Until 2026-10-22 the four steps were four adjectives with no definition, so what the panel's agreement would have measured was agreement on vocabulary.

questions.text: How could a model win on this criterion without the note being better, and where could measuring one harm a client? Asked once, under the table, not per item: the rater names the criterion and says how.
scale: free text, once per rater, naming the criteria it applies to
questions.shown_with: A worked example from this project's own data: a one-sentence note scores 1.00 on economy, so grading economy by itself rewards writing almost nothing. The example the column carried until 2026-10-22 was invented -- a model graded on non-stigmatising language stopping its record of risk -- and does not follow, because recording risk is a clinical description and not a label on a person.
questions.effect: a criterion named here is reported with the flag and is not measured in this round whatever its relevance count, and the reason is kept verbatim

questions.text: What important property of a note is missing from this list?
scale: free text, once per rater, not per item
questions.effect: a property named here enters the pool as a candidate with the rater as its origin, and is rated in a second round if the panel is asked again. The question itself is Lynn's (1986) recommendation, 'The experts, in addition to judging each item, should identify any area(s) that have been omitted from the instrument', which this project had written without knowing.

retention_rule.what_registered_means_here: recorded in this tracked protocol before use. The project has no external preregistration at all: registration.status is not_registered and local_timestamp_is_registration is false. A rule may be amended while no answer exists, which is the case here, and the amendment carries its date.
retention_rule.index: the proportion of the four raters who answer quite or highly relevant

chance_levels_under_a_uniform_rater.null: a rater choosing uniformly among the four points. Nobody behaves like that, so these are a floor for reading the index and not a model of the panel; they are quoted with the null named. Going from three raters to four halves the chance level of the retention rule, which is why the rule did not have to be loosened to accommodate a fourth opinion.

retention_rule.missing_answer: A blank is not an answer, and since 2026-10-22 a rater may say so outright: the scale offers 'nevim', I cannot judge this, coded as missing rather than as a fifth point on the ordinal axis. Either way the index is not computed for that item: it is reported as rated by fewer than four and is not measured. Counting it as not relevant would invent a judgement nobody made, and taking the proportion over the raters who did answer would apply a different rule to that item than to every other -- and an item left blank is likely to be one of the hard ones, so the bias has a direction. What the explicit answer adds is the difference between a criterion that was read and found unjudgeable and one that was skipped.
retention_rule.harm_flag: a criterion any rater names in the harm question is reported with the flag and is not measured in this round whatever its relevance count. Until 2026-10-22 the question was a column and the flag was per item; it is now one answer in which the rater names the criteria, so the flag reads a name rather than a cell.
retention_rule.agreement: Krippendorff's alpha on the ordinal four-point answers over all three raters, with the three pairwise Cohen's kappas beside it. The rule used to name Cohen's kappa alone, which is defined for two raters and could not report the panel it described; S12 recommends kappa over the content validity ratio and index and does not say how to apply it to three. Both are published, with the caveat that three raters over a pool this size give an imprecise estimate, and alpha is the one quoted in prose.
retention_rule.why_the_cut_is_shown_to_the_raters: The sheet already told them what happens to their answers, and a rater who is not told where the line falls guesses. The cost is named rather than avoided: a rater who knows the cut can answer at the extremes to push an item in or out, which is a risk the alternative does not remove, it only hides.
retention_rule.what_the_rule_does_not_do: it does not decide whether an item is measurable, only whether the panel judges it relevant. A relevant item with no operational rule stays unmeasured for that reason and the two reasons are reported apart.
retention_rule.supported_by: Lynn (1986) Table 2, 'Proportion of Experts (Above the Line) Whose Endorsement Is Required to Establish Content Validity Beyond the .05 Level of Significance', whose row for three experts is 1.00. Read on 2026-10-22, the day after this rule was adopted from the chance levels above; the dates are kept so that the agreement can be read as agreement and not as the rule's derivation. See research/gen2/panel-scale-sources.json.
retention_rule.agreement_the_field_expects: Davis (1992) expects of a new instrument that 'investigators should seek 80% or better agreement among reviewers', and counts agreement at both ends of the cut: items both raters put at 1 or 2, plus items both put at 3 or 4. This project reports Krippendorff's alpha over the four ordinal answers, which is stricter and not the same quantity, so the 80% is named as the expectation the field has and not as a threshold this panel is measured against. A percentage agreement computed Davis's way is published beside alpha so that the comparison a reader wants is available.
retention_rule.modified_kappa: Polit, Beck and Owen (2007) proposed a modified kappa that corrects the content validity index for chance agreement, which is the fault this project found in its own rule on 2026-10-21. It is computed and published beside Krippendorff's alpha and the pairwise Cohen's kappas. Its assumption is named wherever it appears: it treats chance endorsement as a coin flip, the same null as the chance levels above, and three raters who share a training and a professional culture are not three coins.
retention_rule.4_of_4: retained for measurement where an operational rule exists
retention_rule.3_of_4_nobody_against: three raters answer quite or highly relevant and the fourth answers somewhat relevant. Published as contested with all four reasons, and not measured in this round. This is the shape MentalHealthBench retains on and this project does not.
retention_rule.3_of_4_one_against: three raters answer quite or highly relevant and the fourth answers not relevant. Published as contested with the dissent given its own weight, and not measured. A yes/no answer could not tell this tier from the one above it, which is what the four points are for.
retention_rule.2_of_4_or_fewer: removed from the measured set; the candidate stays in the catalog with the panel's rating as the reason, which is the same treatment every other unmeasured candidate gets

consequences_recorded_in_advance: The measured set after the panel may differ from the sixteen chosen before it, and the pilot runs on the panel's set.
If the panel retains the criterion the investigator dropped on 2026-10-05, that decision was wrong and the paper says so.
If the panel drops a criterion the assistant proposed, the same applies in the other direction.
A panel of three cannot establish content validity, so the paper claims a screening of the pool by three independent raters and reports the gap that remains.
